https://www.politico.eu/article/france-j.text: PARIS — Far-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon urged his supporters to join nationwide protests on Tuesday in support of students blockading high schools, despite accusations that he instigated violence. “Our country is witnessing the most powerful movement of high school and college students it has seen since May 1968,” Mélenchon said, referring to the massive demonstrations almost 60 years ago that fundamentally reshaped French society. In a nearly 20-minute video published Monday, Mélenchon shrugged off accusations from the government and right-wing politicians that he is inciting unrest by calling for more people to come out in support of students. Vandalism or arson incidents occurred at 24 protests last week, Education Minister Edouard Geffray said Sunday. Advertisement Advertisement The blockades have taken place at 400 to 500 high schools, Geffray added, about 10% of the total in France. The protests began last month when students and teachers blockaded schools, calling for more funding and better working conditions. They have since become a nationwide movement and a political issue as the campaign for next year’s presidential election heats up. “In the field of education, as in all other public services, policies of penny-pinching and budget cuts have led to the near-collapse of the system,” Mélenchon said. Students block the entrance to Saint Charles De Foucauld High School, holding signs denouncing the lack of resources in public education, in Paris on October 5, 2026. | Djoudi Hamani/AFP via Getty Images Mélenchon’s opponents — including France’s historically unpopular government — accuse him of using fiery rhetoric to fuel a febrile political environment that incites violence. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu’s office said the government and intelligence agencies “shared the assessment” that France Unbowed and its ideological allies helped foment the student protests. The 75-year-old has denied encouraging violence — he called the allegation “absurd” in his video and blames the police for brutally dispersing protests — but he’s not backing down from a rhetorical fight. In a blog post over the weekend, Mélenchon made it clear he sees the moment as an opportunity to seize the political narrative, as he did with French debt last month , and push his already strong advantage with the youth vote. Advertisement Advertisement “The government immediately singled out France Unbowed as the devil incarnate. That was a mistake on their part,” he wrote. “It earned us a significant surge in popularity in high schools, where we were already well-received.” A Cluster17 poll shared exclusively with POLITICO before the unrest began last month showed that 47% of respondents younger than 35 planned to vote for Mélenchon. POLITICO’s Poll of Polls aggregator currently shows him with a narrow lead over centrist candidates in the race to finish second and advance to the presidential runoff, where he would likely face off against far-right front-runner Marine Le Pen. Tuesday’s demonstrations could be an important litmus test of how far Mélenchon can turn an autumn of discontent to his advantage. “[Several organizations] have rallied behind the high schoolers and their union. This is absolutely unprecedented. And it’s undoubtedly an indication of a massive protest ahead, one that paves the way for others to follow,” said Paul Vannier, an MP and high-ranking Mélenchon deputy. Yet Mélenchon remains a divisive figure. Seventy-three percent of voters said there was little to no chance they would ever vote for him, according to the Cluster17 poll shared exclusively with POLITICO, compared with 62% for Le Pen. His goal for now is to consolidate his base and make the runoff, and younger voters are a key part of that effort, but images of high schools ablaze and clashes between police and protesters threaten to hurt his standing with the wider electorate. A poll last week found that most respondents agreed the demonstrations were justified but disagreed with France Unbowed’s strategy. Advertisement Advertisement

https://enrsi.stvr.sk/articles/news/4649.text: Minimum security standards for hospitals will be introduced shortly, Health Minister Kamil Šaško (Hlas-SD) told journalists on Thursday following Tuesday's (13 October) attack on a nurse at a hospital in Bratislava's Kramare district. Šaško described the incident as unacceptable and called for exemplary punishment. "Within a short time, minimum standards will be introduced, regardless of the cost, and every hospital will be required to comply with them," the minister declared, noting that security standards currently vary between hospitals. He pointed out that, at some facilities, for example, the duties of private security personnel include refraining from intervening against individuals and focusing instead on protecting the premises. Bratislava University Hospital said on Thursday that a drunk man physically assaulted a 23-year-old nurse in the emergency department of its Kramare hospital on Tuesday. The nurse sustained facial injuries, scratches, bruising and swelling, as well as psychological harm. Police have charged a 63-year-old Austrian man over the incident. A motion seeking his remand in custody is also being prepared. The Bratislava Regional Prosecutor's Office confirmed the charge to TASR, with its spokeswoman, Gabriela Kovacova, saying that, following instructions from the Bratislava regional prosecutor, a motion will be filed to remand the accused in custody on grounds of flight risk and to prevent further offending.
